issues.legal_issue: A settlement causes property to be deemed to pass on the settlor’s death only when an interest for a period ending at death is reserved or the settlor retains a power to restore or reclaim the property.
material_facts: The deceased settled the properties absolutely on the beneficiaries, who received them during his lifetime.
The deeds did not reserve an interest in the properties to the deceased or give him a power to reclaim the properties or their possession.
The beneficiaries did not become entitled to the properties only after the deceased’s death.
issues.conclusion: The settlement properties did not fall within section 12 and were not deemed to pass on the deceased’s death under that section.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1) of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 applies where a settlement reserves to the settlor, expressly or by implication, an interest for life or another period ending at death, or reserves a power to restore or reclaim the absolute interest. None of those conditions was present here.

predicates.settlement_estate_duty_case: The proceeding concerns whether property transferred by settlement is included in the estate for duty on the settlor’s death.
predicates.beneficiaries_entitled_during_settlors_l: The beneficiaries became entitled to the settled property during the settlor’s lifetime.
predicates.interest_reserved_until_death: The settlor retained an interest in the settled property for life or for a period ending at death.
predicates.power_to_reclaim_property: The settlor retained a power to restore or reclaim the settled property or its possession.

issues.definition: When an estate-duty settlement proceeding concerns property that beneficiaries received during the settlor’s lifetime, and the settlor reserved neither an interest ending at death nor a power to reclaim the property, the property is not deemed to pass on the settlor’s death.

issues.legal_issue: A donor’s unsecured right to payments or maintenance does not make gifted property pass on the donor’s death when the donor retains no benefit in the property or its possession.
material_facts: The deeds to the sons and grandsons required annual payments to the deceased, and the deed to the daughter required maintenance for the deceased and his wife.
Those payment and maintenance obligations were not charged on the settled properties.
The deeds transferred the properties absolutely and gave the beneficiaries full power of alienation.
The deceased retained no interest or benefit in the settled properties or in their possession.
issues.conclusion: Section 10 did not apply, and none of the gifted properties or any part of them was liable to be included in the estate on the basis of the payment and maintenance provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, the donee must immediately assume bona fide possession and enjoyment of the gifted property and retain it to the entire exclusion of the donor and of any benefit to the donor. These conditions are cumulative: George Da Costa v. Controller of Estate Duty, Mysore. The words “by contract or otherwise” refer to a legal obligation or an equivalent transaction enforceable at law or in equity. A taxing provision reasonably capable of more than one interpretation must be construed beneficially to the subject, and the court may not add words to it. Because the obligations were unsecured and did not leave the donor with a benefit in the property or its possession, section 10 did not apply.

predicates.gift_estate_duty_case: The proceeding concerns whether property transferred by gift is included in the donor’s estate for duty on the donor’s death.
predicates.donees_received_absolute_gifts: The donor transferred the property absolutely to the donees, who received full power to deal with it.
predicates.payment_or_maintenance_obligations_unsec: The gift documents required payments or maintenance for the donor but did not secure those obligations against the gifted property.
predicates.donor_retained_no_benefit_in_property_or: The donor retained no benefit in the gifted property or in its possession.

issues.definition: In an estate-duty proceeding concerning a gift, absolute transfer accompanied only by unsecured payment or maintenance obligations, with no benefit retained in the property or its possession, means the gifted property is not included on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A deed that merely expresses a hope that the recipient will support the donor does not reserve an enforceable benefit in the gifted property.
material_facts: The deed to the deceased’s wife stated that he hoped she would support him during his lifetime.
The statement created no enforceable liability.
issues.conclusion: No part of the property settled on the wife could be included in computing the value of the estate that passed on the deceased’s death.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, a retained benefit must arise from a legal obligation or an equivalent transaction enforceable at law or in equity; a mere hope or expectation does not suffice. The Court’s construction of section 10 is consistent with George Da Costa v. Controller of Estate Duty, Mysore.

issues.definition: In an estate-duty proceeding concerning a gift, a deed that expresses only a nonbinding hope of support means the gifted property is excluded from the estate value.
